lesson.title: Naming the Suspects: Critical Numbers
lesson.summary: A critical number is the specific x-value of a critical point, the input value produced by a systematic search of a function's derivative, and this section works through finding a pair of them for a cubic polynomial.
lesson.body:
The terms critical point and critical number are closely related, and different textbooks use them slightly differently, so it is worth being precise. Some sources use critical point to mean the location on the graph, the pair (c, f(c)), while critical number refers just to the input value c by itself. Others use the two terms interchangeably. Either way, when a problem asks you to list the critical numbers of a function, it wants a list of x-values, and when it asks for critical points, it may want the corresponding (x, y) pairs. Reading the question carefully matters here.

Finding the critical numbers of a function is a systematic procedure. First, compute the derivative f'(x). Second, note the domain of f, since a critical number must be a value that f itself is actually defined at. Third, solve the equation f'(x) = 0 for x, keeping only solutions inside the domain of f. Fourth, separately identify any x-values in the domain of f where f'(x) fails to exist. The union of the results from steps three and four is the complete list of critical numbers.

Work through a fresh polynomial, f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 5. Since f is a polynomial, its domain is all real numbers, so there is no concern about the derivative being undefined anywhere, the derivative of a polynomial is itself a polynomial, always defined. That means every critical number here will come from step three alone. Differentiate: f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 12. Factor out the common factor of 6 first: f'(x) = 6(x^2 - x - 2). The quadratic x^2 - x - 2 factors as (x - 2)(x + 1), since -2 times 1 equals -2 and -2 plus 1 equals -1, so f'(x) = 6(x - 2)(x + 1). Setting this equal to zero: 6(x - 2)(x + 1) = 0, which happens exactly when x = 2 or x = -1. Both values are real numbers and both lie in the domain of f, which is every real number, so both qualify.

The critical numbers of f are therefore x = -1 and x = 2. If the corresponding critical points, the (x, y) pairs, are wanted instead, compute the outputs: f(-1) = 2(-1)^3 - 3(-1)^2 - 12(-1) + 5 = -2 - 3 + 12 + 5 = 12, and f(2) = 2(2)^3 - 3(2)^2 - 12(2) + 5 = 16 - 12 - 24 + 5 = -15. So the critical points are (-1, 12) and (2, -15).

Notice what finding the critical numbers has, and has not, accomplished. It has narrowed an infinite domain down to exactly two suspects for local extrema. It has not yet said whether x = -1 is a local maximum, a local minimum, or, as the previous section's warning about x^3 showed is entirely possible, neither. That classification job belongs to the First Derivative Test, a few sections ahead. First, the next two sections look more closely at the two separate doorways through which a critical number can arise, f'(x) = 0 and f'(x) undefined, since they call for different algebraic techniques and, later, different geometric pictures.
